The law includes penalties for hospitals with high numbers of patients who are readmitted to the hospital within 30 days of discharge. These penalties, known as the "admission penalty," or readmission penalty, vary by year but can exceed 1 percent of their total Medicare reimbursements for inpatient care. The objective is to have patients continue care in their homes or in outpatient settings rather than be readmitted to the hospital within 30 days to make the most cost effective use of care

original: hearing.The case is about the appointment of former secretary finance by the government through presidential ordinance in 2012. Additional Attorney General Ahsan Ullah Tarar, who is representing the NAB prosecution team, requested the bench to remove the CJP's sister-in-law from the bench.The bench approved the request and removed the CJP's sister-in-law from the bench. said the U.N. nuclear agency had been working to resolve the stalled probe into allegations that Iran was pursuing an atomic weapons program before it signed its landmark nuclear deal with world powers in 2015. The investigation was suspended in December 2014, but a new team has since been appointed.
A senior diplomat at the International Atomic Energy Agency said the team had been tasked with "identifying, collecting and evaluating information on potential undeclared nuclear material and nuclear-related activities by Iran in past years." The diplomat spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to provide details.
The Vienna-based agency said its director general, Yukiya Amano, and Iranian nuclear chief Ali Akbar Salehi discussed cooperation in launching the investigation during talks in Vienna on Thursday, and that Amano had told Salehi that he hoped "the work could be resumed in early 2017."
Neither the agency nor Amano provided details about the scope of the inquiry, its agenda or any suspected Iranian nuclear activities.

s finally time for Tina Fey to hang up her “Weekend Update” anchor’s suit, and head off to her next act. The 40-year-old actress, writer and producer has announced that after 22 seasons on Saturday Night Live she’s retiring from the show. “I am leaving with a heavy heart,” Fey told NBC’s Matt Lauer in a Thursday interview. “I’m not really sure what I’m doing next, but I’ve decided that this season will be my last. And I’m not sure I’ll ever do it again.”

It is a bit of a surprise, but not really. I’ve known Tina for almost two decades now and we’re as close as two friends can be. I’ve grown to admire her as a writer, as a mother and as a person as much as a TV star.

premise for "Chalk the Walk," an event organized by the North Naples Historical Society and Art League of Collier County that encourages kids to draw or paint on sidewalks around the village.
"It's really fun to see all of the kids interacting with the walls," said Susan Pieschek, events coordinator for the North Naples Historical Society and Art League of Collier County. "We have so many beautiful paintings and great chalk drawings."
Chalk the Walk takes place the first Saturday of the month in October, November and December. The event kicks off 8 a.m. at the North Naples Historical Museum, and children are encouraged to draw their own chalk designs at various downtown locations. The public is invited to join in the fun from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m.

This is the scene of one of the most unusual – and potentially threatening – military exercises taking place in Europe in years.

The Polish military is training its troops to smash windows and use crowbars to remove the iron bars used to secure bunkers and fortifications built during the Soviet Union’s occupation of this region, three decades ago.

During the Soviet Union’s occupation of Poland, from 1792 to 1990, the Prussian province of Sanok, which includes the city of Sanok, was the site of a major fortification. The site was transformed into a U.S. military base when the Soviet Union collapsed, and troops continue to train here.

But now there is a plan to bring back the Soviet walls of Sanok, and the Polish government is investing in a plan to see that this long-closed military base is transformed into a major tourist destination, complete with restaurants and art installations, to boost the local economy.

It is a little over two months since the Supreme Court decided to shut down all of Pakistan's plastic factories after a BBC documentary exposed how they are polluting the environment.

Since then, the authorities have started taking action. But there's been a massive surge in the use of plastic containers. The ones being exported are being sent from Karachi, Balochistan and Punjab. The area of Karachi where the factories have been allowed to stay open is a major hub for these goods, and Landhi is a major entry point.

The military occupation is in its fourth decade. These are just a handful of facts of life in Gaza for ordinary Gazans.

If the UN agency for Palestinian refugees were to shut down, the next step will be the destruction of water infrastructure and desalination plants, and the elimination of the water supply to Gaza. The endgame will be the elimination of water altogether. The only water supply to Gaza will be that provided to Gaza by Egypt. There will be no safe drinking water for Gazans, and no way to reverse the water crisis. The Israeli government is not going to give Gaza any of their water, and is not going to tell the people of Gaza to shut down their own desalination plants.

This is a call to action to anyone who cares about the people of Gaza to make your voice heard.

posted photos of their teen-agers unzipping their bags as they moved into dorms or fraternity houses.
One friend had even included his son’s face, as if he were getting a puppy — except, that’s what I felt like.
I’d just been to Nashville to watch my younger son, David, move in to his dorm room at the University of Tennessee at Martin. He’s studying to be an engineering major there.
I had been dreading this day for years. I knew I wanted my kids to have the experience of moving to college like I had. I wanted them to have their first roommate experience and room-search for the college they wanted.
And now I had to face this dreaded day when my older son, Anthony, decided to make the move from high school to college.
It was like the first of many of those “where did they go?” moments. And there would be many more
